case_name: Griffin c. Commission scolaire régionale Blainville Deux-Montagnes
text:
Quebec Superior Court

Citation: Griffin v. Commission scolaire
régionale Blainville Deux-Montagnes

Date: 1989-10-2

Bishop J.

Counsel:

Roger Gervais
, for applicant.

Mario
du
Mesnil
, for respondent,
Commission
Scolaire

Régionale
Blainville Deux-Montagnes.

Allan R. Hilton
and
Colin Irving
, for respondent, Laurenval School
Board.

Jean-Yves Bernard
, for respondent, Attorney-General of Quebec.

[
1
]

Bishop
J.:—By his amended motion for a declaratory judgment under
art. 453 of the
Code of Civil Procedure
, R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-25 (C.P.),
the applicant Griffin asks that an agreement entered into between respondents
Commission Scolaire Régionale Blainville Deux-Montagnes (hereinafter the
"C.S.R. Blainville") and the Laurenval School Board (hereinafter the
"Laurenval S.B.") under s. 450 of the
Education Act
, R.S.Q.
1977, c. I-14, be declared
ultra vires
their powers, and that the court
declare that Mr. Griffin has the right to have his children educated in a
Catholic school, in the English language, under the management and control of
English speaking Catholics.

[
2
]

More specifically, these five
conclusions ask that the court:

1.
Declare

ultra vires the powers of the Commission scolaire régionale Blainville Deux-Montagnes
and the Commission scolaire Laurenval to enter into the agreement dated
February 20th, 1986 and ultra vires the powers of the Minister of Education to
sanction the said agreement;

2.
Declare

that the said interconfessional school board agreement violates the
rights of English speaking Catholics under
section 2
,
15
and
23
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
and section 10 of the
Quebec Charter of
Human Rights and Freedoms
;

3.
Declare

that the Petitioner has a right to have his children educated in a
Catholic school under the authority, management, direction and control of a
Catholic school commission;

4.
Declare

that the Petitioner has a right to have his children educated in the
English language in classes of instruction under the authority, managment and
control of members of the English language minority;

5.
Declare

that English Catholics have the right to have their children educated in
English Catholic schools under the authority, management, direction and control
of members of the English language minority.

I. THE PARTIES AND A FACTUAL SUMMARY

[
3
]

Mr. Griffin's mother tongue is English
and his religion is Roman Catholic. He has four school-age children: Amanda
(aged 13); Brandon (aged 11); and Andrew and Christopher (twins, aged 7); all
of whom attend school in the Province of Quebec and whose mother tongue and
religion are the same as their father's. It is admitted that Mr. Griffin has
the right under ss. 23(1) of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
(Canada Act 1982
(U.K.), c. 11, Schedule B, the "Canada Charter")
to have his children receive primary and secondary school instruction in Quebec
in the English language, subject to s. 23(3) thereof.

[
4
]

Mr. Griffin lives in the County of
Deux-Montagnes, which is not subject to the jurisdiction of the Montreal
Catholic and Protestant school boards. He lives within the jurisdiction of, and
pays his school taxes, to the local Roman Catholic school board of
Deux-Montagnes ("C.S. Deux-Montagnes"), most of whose students are
Roman Catholic and French speaking. His children are registered as Catholics
for school purposes.

[
5
]

The eldest child, Amanda, received her
elementary education in the French language at Ecole Lac des Deux-Montagnes, which
is an elementary school controlled by C.S. Deux-Montagnes, a Catholic related
board.

[
6
]

Secondary schooling in the French
language is provided in the Deux-Montagnes, St. Eustache and Ste. Therese areas
by C.S.R. Blainville, which is a regional school board with Roman Catholic ties
established under s. 423
et seq.
of the
Education Act
, R.S.Q.
1977, c. I-14. The regional board's members are the three local school boards
for the said areas, including C.S. Deux-Montagnes.

[
7
]

When the present motion was first filed
in March 1986, Amanda was registered with C.S.R. Blainville, but was in fact
attending the Lake of Two Mountains High School (the "L.T.M. High
School"), which is controlled by Laurenval S.B., a Protestant related
English language school (for further details thereof
c.f.
admissions of
February 10, 1989). This high school is situated only two kilometers from
Amanda's home.

[
8
]

In 1984-85, 245 of the 547 students at
L.T.M. High School (or 44.8%), were declared to be Roman Catholics, 243 (or
44.4%) were declared to be Protestant, and the balance of 59 (or 10.8%) were of
other religions or of none. In 1988, 220 of the 486 students at L.T.M. High
School (or 45.3%) were Catholics who had been sent there from C.S.R. Blainville
(file No. 28).

[
9
]

Amanda attended L.T.M. High School in
virtue of transfer agreements signed annually since 1969 between C.S.R.
Blainville and Laurenval S.B. pursuant to s. 450 of the
Education Act
(
c.f.

P-1 in file No. 1, P-3 in file No. 3, and files Nos. 49, 51, 52, 54). Such
agreements affect some 40,000 students of all religious denominations (
c.f.

admissions sections 12 and 16, file No. 66) annually in various localities
throughout Quebec where the number of students does not justify the provision
of new school facilities (DL-2, file No. 61).

[
10
]

The 1985-86 transfer agreement (P-1,
file No. 1) provided that Laurenval S.B. would provide secondary schooling in
the English language to English speaking Catholic students under the
jurisdiction of C.S.R. Blainville. About 482 such students from C.S.R. Blainville
were so transferred in 1985-86, and about 341 in 1987-88. Another 404 English
Catholic students were sent to Laurenval S.B. for secondary education in
1987-88 from four other French speaking school boards in the area.

[
11
]

Sections 8 to 11 of this transfer
agreement oblige Laurenval S.B. to provide to Catholic students:

(i) religious instruction during
school hours approved by a Catholic committee and taught by Catholic teachers
of three periods of 50 minutes each every six school days; and

(ii) additional religious services
and extra-curricular activities ("animation pastorale") given by
trained Catholics approved by the bishop of the diocese two days out of every
six; these activities were provided both to the students and to assist the Catholic
teachers who gave religious instructions (
c.f.
files Nos. 56 and 57, and
section 33 of the C.S.R. Blainville's declaration of May 5, 1988 — which is
admitted).

[
12
]

The parties have admitted that the
English Catholic students at Laurenval S.B. receive the same religious
instruction and "animation pastorale" as the French Catholic students
at C.S.R. Blainville (admissions of November 18, 1988, in file No. 69, and
declaration of May 5, 1988 — paras. 10 and 11, and 18 to 23). About 1035 of the
7200 students at Laurenval S.B. in 1986-87 were Roman Catholics.

[
13
]

The parties have also admitted that
this transfer agreement with Laurenval was not exclusive, and that, if an
English Catholic student at C.S.R. Blainville asked to attend another English
school board, C.S.R. Blainville would take the necessary steps to give effect
to the request, subject to the acquiescence of such other English board (
c.f.

admissions of November 18, 1988, and para. 9 of the declaration of May 5,
1988). The parties have further admitted that Mr. Griffin made no complaint to
C.S.R. Blainville with respect to the Laurenval transfer agreement prior to the
institution of the present proceedings, and that, if he had objected to
Laurenval, his children would have been sent to an English Catholic school board
or to a private school (
c.f.
admissions of November 18, 1988, and paras.
12, 13 and 14 of the declaration of May 5, 1988).

[
14
]

On September 28, 1987, about 18 months
after the filing of the present motion, the executive committee of C.S.R.
Blainville adopted a resolution (file No. 48) stating its intention in
principle to enter into an agreement with the Chomedey-Laval School Board, a
Catholic related board, to permit English speaking Catholic students under
C.S.R. Blainville's jurisdiction, including Mr. Griffin's children, to receive
at Chomedey-Laval S.B. a secondary education in English, beginning in the
1987-88 school year.

[
15
]

On October 25, 1988, C.S.R. Blainville
signed an agreement with Chomedey-Laval S.B. under s. 450 by which the latter
agreed to provide secondary education to 69 of the former's English speaking
students (DF-3, file No. 70). One of these students was Brandon Griffin, who is
taking his first year at the secondary level. As of January, 1989, Amanda
Griffin also became a student at Chomedey-Laval S.B. (admissions of February 7,
1989, file No. 69). The average distance from the homes of the students of C.S.
Deux-Montagnes to Chomedey-Laval S.B. is less than 20 kilometers; it is a
30-minute school bus ride.

II. THE PROCEDURES

[
16
]

Mr. Griffin's original motion was dated
March 26, 1986. It invoked his rights under
s. 93
of the
British North
America Act, 1867
(now the
Constitution Act, 1867
) and under s. 23
of the Canada Charter. He amended his motion on November 27, 1987, to add
paras. 24(a) to (g), with a related conclusion, invoking discrimination under
ss. 2 and 15 of the Canada Charter and s. 10 of the Quebec
Charter of Human
Rights and Freedoms
, R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-12 (the "Quebec Charter").

[
17
]

Written contestations of Mr. Griffin's
motion were filed by respondents, the Attorney-General of Quebec, the Ministère
de l'Education and Laurenval S.B., after the motion of the first two
respondents to dismiss Mr. Griffin's motion was rejected on October 17, 1986.
C.S.R. Blainville filed a lengthy statement of facts dated May 5, 1988, which
has been admitted by the parties and in which it asked that its declaration be "accueillie
... à toutes fins que de droit ... sans conclusion de débouté quant à la
demande ... et tout en continuant ... de s'en remettre à la justice".

[
18
]

A hearing on the original motion took place
before Mr. Justice Charles Gonthier on September 18, 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25,
1987. Following this hearing, Mr. Griffin made two motions, one to amend his
motion to add further references to the two Charters and the other to reopen
the hearing. Both motions were granted, the latter on April 11, 1988. Before
the new hearing was held, Mr. Justice Gonthier was named to the Court of
Appeal, and the undersigned was appointed to hear the amended motion on the
merits. Preparatory conferences held on October 13 and December 30, 1988, resulted
in agreements which restricted the proof to the transcripts and documents
referred to in the undersigned's letter to the parties' attorneys of January
26, 1989.

III. MR. GRIFFIN'S CONTENTIONS

[
19
]

In support of his motion, Mr. Griffin
relies upon a combination of the following principal arguments:

(1) He and other Roman Catholics
were granted rights and privileges under
s. 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

that entitle them to have their children educated in Roman Catholic schools
established and controlled by them. This contention is an essential one, and
was the object of most of the parties' arguments.

[
20
]

To succeed on this contention, Mr.
Griffin must first establish that in 1867 the Roman Catholic inhabitants in the
municipality where he now lives were a "class of persons" which had
been granted "by law" rights and privileges with respect to
"denominational schools". He must in this regard circumvent or
distinguish a decision of the Privy Council which is unfavourable to his
contention, namely,
Hirsch v. Protestant Board of School Com'rs of Montreal
,

1928 CanLII 500 (UK JCPC)
,
[1928] 1 D.L.R. 1041
,
[1928] A.C. 200
,
48 Que. K.B. 115
(hereinafter referred
to as
"Hirsch"
). Mr. Griffin must then establish that s. 450
of the
Education Act
and the transfer agreements entered into thereunder
have "prejudically affected" these rights or privileges.

(2) Secondly, Mr. Griffin maintains
that English speaking Roman Catholics have the right, under s. 23(1) of the
Canada Charter, to require that their children receive secondary education in
the English language in Quebec, and, under s. 23(3)(
b
) thereof, that
such education be publicly funded and controlled by English speaking Roman
Catholics.

(3) Thirdly, Mr. Griffin maintains
that he and other English speaking Roman Catholics in Quebec, as a group, are
subject to discrimination because their children may be required under the
transfer agreement to attend schools managed by Protestant school boards over
which such group has no control, the whole in contravention of ss. 2(
a
)
and 15(1) of the Canada Charter, and of s. 10 of the Quebec Charter. In
contrast, the children of French speaking Roman Catholics or of English
speaking Protestants are free to attend schools controlled by school boards of
their parents' respective faiths, whose commissioners are elected directly or
indirectly by such parents.

IV. MR. GRIFFIN'S RIGHTS UNDER S. 93 OF THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1867

[
21
]

Section 93(1) and (2) read as follows:

93. In and for each Province the
Legislature may exclusively make Laws in relation to Education, subject and
according to the following Provisions:—

(1) Nothing in any such Law shall
prejudically affect any Right or Privilege with respect to Denominational
Schools which any Class of Persons have by Law in the Province at the Union:

(1) All the Powers, Privileges, and
Duties at the Union by Law conferred and imposed in Upper Canada on the
Separate Schools and School Trustees of the Queen's Roman Catholic Subjects
shall be and the same are hereby extended to the Dissentient Schools of the
Queen's Protestant and Roman Catholic Subjects in Quebec:

A. Applicable provisions of s. 93

[
22
]

The opening words of s. 93 give the
provincial legislature full and exclusive power to make laws in relation to
education in the province, "subject and according to" the provisions
which follow. Subsection (1) protects certain rights and privileges of certain
persons from the prejudicial effect of such laws.

[
23
]

All of the following conditions must be
met in order to claim the protection of s. 93(1):

(a) there must be a right or
privilege with respect to denominational schools;

(b) which a particular class of
persons has;

(c) by law;

(d) in the province of Quebec at the
time of the Union in 1867; and

(e) which is prejudicially affected
by a law made by the Quebec legislature:
c.f. A.-G. Que. v. Greater Hull
School Board

(1984),
1984 CanLII 29 (SCC)
,
15 D.L.R. (4th) 651
at p. 657,
[1984] 2 S.C.R. 575
,
28
M.P.L.R. 146
, hereinafter referred to as
"Greater Hull"
).

[
24
]

The words "by law" in s.
93(1) have generally been interpreted by the courts as referring to statutes.
In
Greater Montreal Protestant School Board v. Que. (A.-G.)

(1989),
1989 CanLII 125 (SCC)
,
57
D.L.R. (4th) 521
at pp. 536-7,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 377
,
92 N.R. 327
(hereinafter
referred to as
"P.S.B.G.M.
—
1989"
), the Supreme Court
of Canada stated:

The
text which sets out the
exception is plain: the expression "by Law" and "at the
Union" limit the protection to rights and privileges established by
statutes in force at the time of the Confederation.

[
25
]

The parties to the present litigation
have proceeded on the basis that the relevant pre-Confederation statute as to
education applicable to the province of Quebec is the
Act respecting
Provincial Aid for Superior Education
, —
Normal and Common Schools
,
C.S.L.C. 1861, c. 15 (hereinafter the "1861 Act"). This statute was
considered in detail at p. 660
et seq.
in
Greater Hull
,
in
Hirsch

and
in P.S.B.G.M. — 1989.

[
26
]

The principal question at issue under
s. 93(1), therefore, is whether in 1867 Roman Catholics were a class of persons
who had, in the area where Mr. Griffin now resides and pursuant to the 1861
Act, rights or privileges with respect to denominational schools.

[
27
]

The decided cases do not contain a
definition of the words "denominational schools". The 1971 Compact
Edition of the Oxford English Dictionary gives the following definitions:

denominational
: 1. Belonging to, or of the nature of, a denomination or
ecclesiastical sect; sectarian, as a denominational school or college; hence
denominational system of education, one providing or recognizing such schools,
etc.

denomination
: ... 5. A collection of individuals classed together under
the same name; now almost always spec. a religious sect or body having a common
faith and organization, and designated by a distinctive name.

B. Analysis of the Hirsch decision

[
28
]

In
Hirsch
, the Privy Council had
to determine whether certain provisions of a 1903 Quebec statute were
intra
vires.
This statute granted the children of persons professing the Jewish
religion the same rights, privileges and obligations for school purposes as
Protestant children.

[
29
]

The Privy Council asked the following
questions [at p. 1046]:

... first, whether any and which of
the schools referred to in that [1903] statute were denominational schools in
which any class of persons had by law any right or privilege at the Union, and,
secondly, whether and to what extent that statute prejudicially affects any
such right or privilege.

[
30
]

The Privy Council decided that the
dissentient schools in the "rural areas" outside the Cities of
Montreal and Quebec should be considered as the "denominational
schools" envisaged by s. 93(1) for the following reasons [at p. 1047]:

Where a school is founded by a body
of Protestants and is maintained by their contributions and managed by trustees
appointed by them, where its teachers are chosen by those trustees after
examination by a Protestant Board of Examiners, where its religious books are
selected by the Protestant minister and admission to the school is confined
(except by favour) to the children of Protestant parents, it would be affectation
to call that school anything but a denominational school; and the same is
equally true of a like dissentient school under Roman Catholic control. It is
plain also that the dissentient supporters of such a school, who are bound
together by a common religious faith, form a "class of persons"
having special rights and privileges with respect to the school, including the
right to appoint the managing trustees and through those trustees to select the
teachers at the school, to control the course of study and to exclude children
of another faith.

[
31
]

The Privy Council concluded, however,
that the "common school" in a "rural area" was not such a
"denominational school" because [at pp. 1047-8]:

Such a [common] school, if in a
single school district, is under the management of commissioners appointed by
the whole body of landholders and householders in the district without regard
to their religious faith; and even in a district where a minority has
established its own separate school, the electors who remain need not be all of
the same religious persuasion. No doubt it is true, as stated by the Canadian
Courts, that in most of the school districts in the rural area the majority of
the landholders and householders are Roman Catholics, and, accordingly, that
the common schools in those districts (other than the dissentient schools) are
in fact controlled by members of that religious community; but, if so, the
result is due to the circumstances of the particular school districts, and it
is not a right or privilege to which any class of persons are "by
law" entitled.

[
32
]

The Privy Council then decided that the
"common schools" in the Cities of Montreal and Quebec, which were
governed by different provisions of the 1861 Act, should also be considered as
"denominational schools" with respect to which the Roman Catholics or
Protestants in each city constituted a class of persons having rights or
privileges under s. 93(1). The reasons given were as follows [at pp. 1049-50]:

Every common school in either city
was under the management and control of a board of commissioners chosen from
persons of a particular religious faith, and each of these boards is referred
to (in s. 131) as "representing" a religious persuasion. The school
fund contributed by the corporation was to be apportioned between the two
boards in proportion to the religious persuasions which they respectively
represented, and therefore roughly (although not precisely) according to the
religious faiths of those who contributed to the fund. The examination of
teachers, the selection of religious books, and the right to visit the schools
were based on a like separation of faiths. It is true that in the two cities a
school belonging to either board might before the date of Confederation be
attended by children of a faith different from that represented by the board;
but it appears to their Lordships that the provisions for the management and
control of the schools by persons of a particular religious persuasion set upon
them a denominational stamp which could not be effaced by the attendance of a
certain number of children of a divergent faith.

[
33
]

It is common ground in the present case
that, in 1867, the school municipality then comprising the territory where Mr.
Griffin now resides was in a "rural area", that is outside the Cities
of Montreal and Quebec, and that, in such territory, there were then no
dissentient Roman Catholic school trustees, as permitted under s. 55
et seq.

of the 1861 Act. In 1871, a census disclosed that there were 532 Protestants
and 17,875 Roman Catholics in the County of Deux-Montagnes (para. 26 and
annexes of admissions of September 18, 1987, file No. 66). The Protestants then
constituted only 2.9% of this county's population.

[
34
]

Accordingly, if
Hirsch
is
applicable
, since the Roman Catholic school in Mr. Griffin's municipality in
1867 was a common school, and not a dissentient one, Roman Catholics did not
then have rights or privileges with respect to "denominational
schools" in that area.

C. Applicable provisions of the 1861 Act

[
35
]

These were summarized in detail by the
Privy Council
in
Hirsch
at pp. 1046-7, as follows:

The effect of the statute of 1861
was to establish two somewhat different educational systems, namely, one system
for Lower Canada outside the Cities of Quebec and Montreal (which may be
referred to as the "rural area") and another system for those two
cities.

In the rural area there were set up
two classes of school for the elementary instruction of youth, that is to say,
(
a
) in each municipality, one or more common schools managed by school
commissioners elected by all the landholders and householders of the
municipality other than the dissentient inhabitants to be hereafter referred
to, and (
b
) in any municipality in which any number of inhabitants
professing a religious faith different from that of the majority had signified
such dissent, one or more schools managed by trustees appointed by the
dissentients. These schools were maintained partly by monthly school fees,
partly by allowances out of the common school fund, and partly by a school rate
levied by the school commissioners, or, in the case of dissentients, by their
trustees. The teachers at each school were appointed by the commissioners or
trustees in charge of the school, having first been examined by a board of
examiners for the county, which might (if the Governor-in-Council so ordained)
be organized in two divisions, one Roman Catholic and the other Protestant. The
course of study to be followed in each school was regulated by the
commissioners or trustees (as the case might be), but it was provided (by s. 65
of the Act) that "the curé, priest or officiating minister shall have the
exclusive right of selecting the books having reference to religion and morals
for the use of the schools for children of his own religious faith." The
schools in each municipality were to be visited periodically by visitors
consisting of the resident clergy and other official persons; but no priest,
minister or ecclesiastic was to visit a school belonging to inhabitants not of
his own persuasion except with the consent of the commissioners or trustees of
the school (s. 121). Children from 5 to 16 years of age residing in any school
district were to have a right to attend "the school thereof" upon
payment of the monthly fees (s. 66); but this provision does not appear to have
applied to the dissentient schools, which were reserved (except as a matter of
favour) for children of the dissentient faith residing in the district and (if
there was room) for children from other school districts "of the same faith
as the dissentients for whom the school was established" (s. 56). This
reservation, though not clearly stated in the Act, appears to be deducible from
its terms ...

[
36
]

The following similar short summary was
set out in
Greater Hull
, at p. 660:

The law in Quebec at the time of the
Union was c. 15 of C.S.L.C. 1861, titled the "Act respecting Provincial
Aid for Superior Education, — and Normal and Common Schools" (hereafter
"the 1861 Act"). Under this Act, two systems of education existed,
one for the Cities of Montreal and Quebec and the other for the remainder of
the province (ss. 27
et seq.
and 128
et seq.
of the
1861 Act
).

In Montreal and Quebec common
schools existed open to all children between the ages of five and sixteen.
These schools were directed and controlled by two groups of commissioners, one
Catholic and the other Protestant. All these schools were denominational.

The commissioners were not elected
but appointed by the municipal council.

In
Hirsch
, supra
, the court
observed at p. 1050 D.L.R., p. 212 A.C.:

"The Roman Catholics in
Montreal or Quebec formed a class of persons who had the right and privilege of
having their schools controlled and managed by commissioners of that religious
persuasion and their teachers examined by examiners of the same persuasion; and
like privileges belonged to the Protestants of each city with regard to the
schools controlled by the Protestant Board of Commissioners."

Outside Montreal and Quebec there
were common schools in each municipality, which were also directed and
controlled by school commissioners. These were elected. According to the Privy
Council
decision in
Hirsch
, these schools were non-denominational.

In these municipalities the members
of a minority religious group had the right to create one or more dissentient
schools directed and controlled by trustees elected by them. These dissentient
schools were denominational.

The right of Protestants and
Catholics to direct and control their own denominational schools was therefore
recognized by law at the time of the Union.

The financing came from three
sources: government grants, taxes and school fees. ...

A common schools fund existed, and
school commissioners and trustees were entitled to receive a proportionate
share of this.

D. Applicable provisions of the present Education Act

[
37
]

Under the present
Education Act
,
a school municipality is established by an Order in Council which fixes its
territorial boundaries for administrative purposes. A school municipality
may
,
however, apply only to Roman Catholics or Protestants within such territory (s.
39). Each school municipality contains public schools which are controlled by
commissioners, or, in the case of a dissentient school, by trustees. These
commissioners, or trustees, as the case may be, form a school corporation (ss.
73 and 294) or school board, and are elected by the ratepayers of the
municipality. A dissentient school is composed of a number of ratepayers
"professing a religious belief different from that of the majority of the
ratepayers" within the school municipality who have withdrawn from the
control of the local school board to establish a separate dissentient school
corporation (s. 55
et seq.
). A dissentient ratepayer may not vote for
local school commissioners; and only dissentient ratepayers can vote for local
school trustees (s. 83). The powers and duties of school commissioners and
trustees, or school boards, are set out in ss. 189
et seq.
and 294
et
seq.
Each school corporation levies its own school taxes upon its
ratepayers.

[
38
]

Sections 423 to 450 of the
Education
Act
govern regional school boards. C.S.R. Blainville is a regional school
board. The local school boards who have opted to form part of a regional school
board are the members thereof, and their commissioners are the commissioners or
trustees of the regional school board. The territory of the regional school
board is equivalent to the total territories of its member boards, who may
delegate to it the whole or part of their powers.

[
39
]

Specific sections of the
Education
Act
and of other legislation govern public schools in the Cities of
Montreal and Quebec and adjacent areas, which are controlled by Protestant and
Catholic school boards, termed "confessional school boards", and
defined under s. 1(3.1) of the Act.

[
40
]

Section 450 of the
Education Act

reads, in part:

450. Any school board or regional
board may make, for a fixed period, an agreement whereby children under its
jurisdiction may, at its expense, attend a school of another board or a private

F. Analysis of Mr. Griffin's attacks on Hirsch

(1) Mr. Griffin first invokes the
"large and liberal" interpretation of s. 93(1) as part of the
Canadian Constitution, against a narrow and technical one.

[
46
]

In
P.S.B.G.M.
—
1989
the
majority of the court stated at pp. 535-6:

I am of the view that in this case,
the resolution to the problem is not to be found in one rule of interpretation
as opposed to another. ... It is true, of course, that the fact that the
guarantee is constitutionally entrenched is relevant to its interpretation. As
a constitutional text,
s. 93(1)
may deserve a "purposive"
interpretation but, in so doing, courts must not improperly amplify the
provision's purpose. While it may be rooted in notions of tolerance and
diversity, the exception in s. 93 is not a blanket affirmation of freedom of
religion or freedom of conscience. The entrenched right of specified classes of
persons in a province to enjoy publicly-sponsored denominational schools based
on a fixed statutory benchmark should not be construed as a
Charter
human right
or freedom or, to use the expression of Professor Peter Hogg, a "small
bill of rights for the protection of minority religious groups": see P.
Hogg,
Constitutional Law of Canada
, 2nd ed. (1985), at p. 824. ...

This is not to say that we should
ignore the plain purpose of
s. 93(1)
or ignore its constitutional context.
Wilson J. explained in the
Separate Schools Reference, supra
, at p. 58
D.L.R., p. 1194 S.C.R., that:

"Section 93(1) should ... be
interpreted in a way which implements its clear purpose which was to provide a
firm protection for Roman Catholic education in the Province of Ontario and
Protestant education in the Province of Quebec."

The exception to the provincial
power does confer constitutional rights on specific groups in a specific
manner, in keeping with what Wilson J. characterized as an "historically
important compromise" struck at Confederation. It is true that the rights
or privileges under ordinary law to which
s. 93(1)
refers have been frozen at
Confederation. But just like the basic provincial power which, as Viscount Cave
explained, was not "stereotyped" at the Union, the exception to that
power has also matured over time through judicial interpretation. The approach
courts have taken to the interpretation of the expression "with respect to
Denominational Schools" in cases such as
Hull, supra
, which I will
discuss below, demonstrates that the law in force "at the Union"
cannot on its own set the content of the constitutional right in
s. 93(1)
.

While the text of
s. 93(1)
should of
course be interpreted as a constitutional document, it must not be read in such
a manner as to supplant or frustrate the operation of what Professor Carignan
has called the "mécanisme de constitutionalisation". The very text of

s. 93(1)
instructs courts as to the manner in which content should be given to
the rights and privileges provided for in the exception. As Wilson J. observed,
in the
Separate Schools Reference, supra
, at p. 45 D.L.R., pp. 1177-8
S.C.R., "It must be remembered ... that
s. 93(1)
only protects rights and
privileges guaranteed by law. Our task therefore is to examine the laws in
force prior to Confederation to see what rights and privileges they gave."
The interpretive task is inherently different from that with which courts are
faced when called upon to give content to constitutional rights entrenched in a
document such as the
Charter
. I am wary of deciding cases such as this one on
the basis of one or another method of interpretation rather than the specific
direction provided by the legislator in s. 93(1). Both the restrictive and
liberal methods of interpretation, when misused, wrongly become rhetorical
devices rather than rules of law.

[
47
]

The court shall, in the present case,
therefore, follow the "specific direction provided by the legislator"
in interpreting and applying s. 93(1).

The law in force in the province [of
Ontario] at the time of the Confederation did not confer any legal power on
separate school trustees to choose the language of instruction, although they

guaranteed by

Now, the constitutional right to minority language education created by s. 23

Constitution

No subject has created more

• • • • •

The compromise expressed in s. 23 is

A

[

Plaintiff argues that he and other
English speaking Roman Catholics in Quebec are subject to discrimination
because their children are required, under the transfer agreements, to attend
schools managed by Protestant school boards over which they have no control. He
points out that the children of French speaking Roman Catholics and of English

by such parents. English speaking Roman Catholics in Quebec do not have this

[
94
]

Sections 2(
a
) and 15(1) read as
follows:

2. [
Fundamental freedoms
]
Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(
a
) freedom of conscience and
religion;

• • • • •

15(1) [
Equality before and under
law and equal protection and benefit of law
] Every individual is equal
before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal

[
95
]

Plaintiff has not cited authorities to
justify his contention that the presence of a Roman Catholic child in a
non-Catholic school, with supporting Catholic religious instruction and
"animation pastorale", constitutes
per se
a breach of such
child's right to "freedom of religion" under s.
2(a).

Plaintiff's arguments have been primarily concerned with s. 15(1).

[
96

In
Andrews v. Law Society of B.C.

(1989),
1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
,
56 D.L.R. (4th) 1
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 143
,
34 B.C.L.R. (2d) 273
, the court
(McIntyre J.) stated (at pp. 9-10, 13, 18-9, 24):

Section 15(1)
of the
Charter

provides for every individual a guarantee of equality before and under the law,
as well as the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without
discrimination. This is not a general guarantee of equality, it does not
provide for equality between individuals or groups within society in a general
or abstract sense, nor does it impose on individuals or groups an obligation to
accord equal treatment to others. It is concerned with the application of the
law. No problem regarding the scope of the word "law", as employed in
s. 15(1), can arise in this case because it is an Act of the legislature which
is under attack. Whether other governmental or
quasi
-governmental
regulations, rules or requirements may be termed laws under s. 15(1) should be
left for cases in which the issue arises.

• • • • •

It [equality] is a comparative
concept, the condition of which may only be attained or discerned by comparison
with the condition of others in the social and political setting in which the
question arises. It must be recognized at once, however, that every difference
in treatment between individuals under the law will not necessarily result in
inequality and, as well, that identical treatment may frequently produce
serious inequality ... in this court ...
R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.

(1985),
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
,
18 D.L.R. (4th) 321
at p. 362,
18 C.C.C. (3d) 385
,
[1985] 1 S.C.R. 295

at p. 347,
where Dickson C.J.C. said:

"The equality necessary to
support religious feedom does not require identical treatment of all religions.
In fact, the interests of true equality may well require differentiation in
treatment."

• • • • •

It is not every distinction or
differentiation in treatment at law which will transgress the equality
guarantees of
s. 15
of the
Charter
. It is, of course, obvious that legislatures
may — and to govern effectively — must treat different individuals and groups
in different ways.

• • • • •

I would say then that discrimination
may be described as a distinction, whether intentional or not but based on
grounds relating to personal characteristics of the individual or group, which
has the effect of imposing burdens, obligations, or disadvantages on such
individual or group not imposed upon others, or which withholds or limits
access to opportunities, benefits, and advantages available to other members of
society. ...

The enumerated grounds in s. 15(1)
are not exclusive ... [but] do, however, reflect the most common and probably
the most socially destructive and historically practised bases of
discrimination ... Both the enumerated grounds themselves and other possible
grounds of discrimination recognized under s. 15(1) must be interpreted in a
broad and generous manner reflecting the fact that they are constitutional
provisions not easily repealed or amended but intended to provide a
"continuing framework of the legitimate exercise of governmental
power" and, at the same time, for the "unremitting protection"
of equality rights ...

• • • • •

Where discrimination is found, a
breach of s. 15(1) has occurred and — where s. 15(2) is not applicable — any
justification, any consideration of the reasonableness of the enactment,
indeed, any consideration of factors which could justify the discrimination and
support the constitutionality of the impugned enactment would take place under
s. 1.

[
97
]

In the present case, plaintiff's
complaint arises from the historical fact that school legislation in Lower
Canada at Confederation divided schools and ratepayers on religious lines,
rather than on language lines. It was then assumed that Roman Catholics would
be French speaking and Protestants English speaking. The rights and privileges
of dissentient or minority groups were guaranteed on a religious or
denominational basis by
s. 93(1)
, but without regard to their language. This
division on a religious basis is still preserved in the present
Education
Act
, subject, however, to the exception set out in s. 189(3).

[
98
]

Section 189 sets out the duties of a
school board and provides in s-s. (3) that educational services and courses are
to be provided to all children domiciled in its territory "in conformity
with the Charter of the French Language", also known as Bill 101. Sections
72 to 88 of Bill 101 govern the language of instruction in the schools. Section
72 requires that French be the language of instruction in all schools, except
that English may be such language in the restricted cases set out in s. 73. In
Q.A.P.S.B.

—
1984, supra
, ss. 72 and 73,
inter alia
, were held to be
inconsistent with s. 23 of the Canada Charter, not justified under s. 1
thereof, and hence without effect. In 1986, s. 78.1 was added, which prohibits
a child from being taught in English unless he or she was eligible under s. 73.

[
99

At the present time, however, there
exist in this province, outside of the Cities of Montreal and Quebec, groups of
English speaking Roman Catholics whose right to require an English language
education for their children flow from
s. 23
of the
Charter
, and/or from their
ability to convince their local French speaking Catholic school board either to

100

Education
Act

Education Act.

domicile requirement of s. 82 as discriminating against him. Accordingly, his

discrimination against plaintiff such as to breach s. 15(1), a series of

2. Whether plaintiff's right to the
"equal protection and equal benefit of the law" has been denied by

In
Andrews

stated at pp. 23-4:

... in assessing whether a
complainant's rights have been infringed under s. 15(1), it is not enough to

before and under the law or that the law has a different impact on him or her

religious instruction and "animation pastorale" provided, pursuant to

c.f.
I above), to Roman

In

(1989),

The doctrine of mootness is an
aspect of a general policy or practice that a court may decline to decide a
case which raises merely a hypothetical or abstract question. The general
principle applies when the decision of the court will not have the effect of
resolving some controversy which affects or may affect the rights of the
parties. If the decision of the court will have no practical effect on such
rights, the court will decline to decide the case. This essential ingredient
must be present not only when the action or proceeding is commenced but at the
time when the court is called upon to reach a decision. Accordingly if,
subsequent to the initiation of the action or proceedings, events occur which
affect the relationship of the parties so that no present live controversy
exists which affects the rights of the parties, the case is said to be moot.
The general policy or practice is enforced in moot cases unless the court exercises
its discretion to depart from its policy or practice.

[

new
Education Act
